title: Linking physiological processes to life-history traits and toxic effects: a bioenergetic approach based on DEB theory
text: 1 Information about this project

title: Linking physiological processes to life-history traits and toxic effects: a bioenergetic approach based on DEB theory
text:
1.1 Abstract
Earthworms are key ecosystem engineers whose life-history traits are strongly influenced by environmental conditions and chemical stress. Mechanistic models are therefore needed to integrate these multiple drivers and predict organism responses under realistic exposure scenarios. In this study, we first developed a Dynamic Energy Budget (DEB) model for Aporrectodea caliginosa describing the effects of food availability, population density, and adult isolation on growth, maturation, and reproduction, and subsequently extended this model into a DEB–Toxicokinetic–Toxicodynamic (DEB-TKTD) framework to characterize the effects of imidacloprid and epoxiconazole.
The baseline DEB model was calibrated using literature data and a new density experiment initiated at the juvenile stage. Alternative formulations were compared regarding food acquisition, reserve contribution to fresh body mass, and post-maturation energy allocation. The best-supported formulations combined a progressive change in energy allocation after maturation, a normalized hyperbolic functional response, and a weak contribution of reserves to fresh body mass. Density-dependent reductions in juvenile growth were largely explained by lower food acquisition per individual, while simulations of isolated adults suggested that reproductive energy may be partly redirected toward somatic processes when mating opportunities are absent.
The DEB model was then coupled with previously calibrated two-compartment toxicokinetic models and toxicity data for juvenile growth, adult growth, and reproduction. Toxicodynamic parameters and alternative physiological modes of action were estimated independently for both pesticides. Imidacloprid effects were best described by a combined reduction in assimilation and growth, whereas reduced assimilation alone provided the most parsimonious explanation for epoxiconazole toxicity. Estimated internal tolerance concentrations were substantially lower for imidacloprid than for epoxiconazole, consistently with its greater toxicity across life-history endpoints. The models captured the overall concentration-dependent responses, although systematic deviations remained at high imidacloprid and mortality were not fully represented.
By linking environmental conditions, internal exposure, energetic processes, and life-history responses within a unified framework, this study provides a mechanistic basis for predicting pesticide effects in earthworms and supports future applications to chemical mixtures and multiple environmental stressors.

1.3 How to use this repository ?

1.3.1 Repository organisation
The git repository linked to this website is available here.
Folders containing files concerning directly the study :

data folder : Contains the raw data files with direct notations from the experiments
functions folder : Contains R scripts with general functions used throughout different scripts
quarto folder : Contains all the .qmd files that generate the html pages, and their associated cache and files which cannot be moved to another folder.
mod folder : Contain all the models generated.
photos folder : Contains all photos used in html pages
fig folder : Contains all figure generated by quarto documents
references folder

apa.csl : File of the reference style used for the website
reference.bib : File containing all references from a zotero library


Folders concerning the setup of the git repository and the web pages :

_book : Where the final html pages are created
index.qmd : Home page of the web site (cannot be put in the quarto folder)
_quarto.yaml : YAML file that setup the structure of the website from the quarto (.qmd) documents
_freeze folder : Cache the results of code blocks (code cells) to avoid recalculating them on each execution
.git, .gitignore & .github : Git related folders
.quarto : Store configuration files, metadata, and intermediate files related to a Quarto project
.Rproj.user & Acali-DEB.Rproj : R project related files
appearance folder :

html_css.scss : CSS file to modify the look of the html pages
lightnord.theme : Theme to use for code blocks displayed in the html pages




1.3.2 How to reproduce everything
If you wish to reproduce the results of this study, all you need are available in the quarto folder and the mod folder.
Instructions :

Whether or not you want to run the models again, please delete the folders from the quarto folder that end by _cache or _files and delete all the figures present in the fig folder.

If you do not want to run the models again, move on to the next step
If you wish to run the models again, please delete the files in mod but the .model files and keep the arborescence)

Then, you can render again all .qmd files from the quarto folder in the alphabetical order of their name. Some code line will have to be de-commented for some figures to be rendered again.

2.1.1 Earthworm model - Aporrectodea caliginosa
Aporrectodea caliginosa (Figure 2.1), an endogeic earthworm species, was the chosen biological model for it is considered highly representative of agricultural soil (Bart et al., 2018) and is part of the most sensitive agricultural species to pesticides (Pelosi et al., 2013). It is also a species we are able to cultivate under laboratory conditions (Section 2.1.1.1).






Figure 2.1: Adult A. caliginosa individual.




2.1.1.1 Earthworm cultivation at EcoSys
A further objective of this study is to evaluate the effects of a pesticides mixture on inter-individual variations of life-history traits and behavior of A. caliginosa. To achieve this, it is essential to use individuals whose genetic diversity is representative of a natural population with limited exposure to plant protection products (PPPs). This excludes the use of the breeding stock maintained at EcoSys, as the individuals have been kept in a closed system since the initiation of the breeding program (for over 5 years), with no consideration for maintaining genetic diversity. Therefore, it was necessary to establish a new A. caliginosa breeding population appropriate for the scientific questions addressed in this study.


2.1.1.2 Initially collected individuals.
To initiate the culture, individuals were collected from a natural population in a permanent grassland in Versailles (48°48′ N, 2°5′ E, called “les Closeaux”) where no pesticides have been applied for more than 25 years (Figure 2.2). The individuals were identified using a binocular microscope and an identification key. Ten sampling sessions were conducted in the fall of 2023 and the spring of 2024, yielding a total of 325 individuals.






Figure 2.2: Collection of Aporrectodea caliginosa and Aporrectodea icterica individuals in a meadow at the Château de Versailles and installation of the new culture in our laboratory.




2.1.1.2.1 Workflow
Individuals are bred at 18°C in 1 L vessels in groups of five individuals (Figure 2.2) using a loamy soil texture called Closeaux soil (based on the texture definition of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)), sampled from the same meadow as initial individuals. Pesticides found in the soil are summarized in Figure 2.3 and its general properties in Table 2.1. The soil was collected from the top 0-20 cm, air-dried and crushed to pass a 2 mm mesh. Soil culture is kept with a soil water-holding capacity (WHC) of 60-70%. Individuals are fed with horse dung frost and defrosted twice before being milled (> 1mm) as presented in Lowe & Butt (2005). They are fed each month with the equivalent of around 6 g of dry horse dung which are given with a WHC of 60-70%.

title: 2  Earthworms and pesticides
text:
2.2 Pesticides of interest
Because our aim was to study a mixture of pesticides representative of earthworm exposure in agricultural soils, a crucial step of the study was to select two relevant pesticides.

2.2.1 Choice of Epoxiconazole and Imidacloprid
The selection was made in fall 2023 and was guided by two main criteria: the ubiquity and persistence of pesticide residues in soils, and the availability of ecotoxicological data on earthworms.
Froger et al. (2023) conducted an extensive nationwide survey of pesticide contamination in French soils, monitoring 111 pesticide residues across 47 sites under various land uses. Epoxiconazole and imidacloprid were detected in 47% and 9% of all sites, respectively, with median concentrations of 5.8 ng/g and 2.9 ng/g, and maximum concentrations of 23.6 ng/g and 13.8 ng/g. In arable lands, epoxiconazole, bixafen, fluopyram, fluxapyroxad, glyphosate & AMPA, diflufenican, and terfluthrin were among the most frequently detected compounds.
In a complementary study, Pelosi et al. (2021) investigated the exposure of earthworms to 31 pesticide residues in both treated and untreated habitats within an intensive agricultural landscape in France (Spring 2016, Long-Term Socio-Ecological Research Site, Zone Atelier Plaine & Val de Sèvre). Diflufenican, imidacloprid, boscalid, and epoxiconazole were among the most frequently detected residues, found in more than 80% of sampled soils.
Based on these two studies, we initially targeted a range of pesticide residues. Ultimately, we selected epoxiconazole and imidacloprid due to the availability of toxicological data and their known effects on earthworms (Bart et al., 2019, 2020; Capowiez et al., 2006; Dittbrenner et al., 2010, 2011; Pelosi et al., 2016; Van Loon et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2019). Despite being now banned in the EU, both pesticides continue to be of concern due to their ubiquity and persistence in the environment. These pesticides have been shown to persist in agricultural soils, with concentrations that can still pose adverse effects on non-target organisms, such as earthworms. Imidacloprid is particularly known for impairing earthworm bioturbation, a critical process that supports many ecosystem functions (Chen et al., 2021). Both pesticides’ enduring presence in the environment highlights the relevance of studying their long-term ecological impacts. This choice aligns with the objectives of the EEWORM ANR project, which aims to investigate the eco-evolutionary dynamics of earthworms under pesticide exposure and the resulting impacts on ecosystem functions.

2.2.2 Epoxiconazole (EPX)
Epoxiconazole (EPX) is a broad-spectrum fungicide from the azole family, used to control plant diseases caused by Ascomycetes, Basidiomycetes, and Deuteromycetes (Lewis et al., 2006). It was commercialized by BASF SE in 1993 and applied to a variety of crops including cereals, soy, bananas, rice, coffee, beets, and turnips (Lewis et al., 2006). Epoxiconazole has also been investigated for medical applications due to its antifungal properties, although its primary use has remained agricultural (Hamdi et al., 2022).
In France, EPX was widely applied on cultivated land, primarily as a foliar treatment. Before its withdrawal, approximately 200 tons were sold annually. Its market authorization was revoked by ANSES in 2019, and subsequently at the EU level in 2020.
Epoxiconazole is a sterol biosynthesis inhibitor (SBI) (Lewis et al., 2006). It disrupts fungal metabolism by inhibiting mycelial growth, reducing conidia production, and limiting mycotoxin synthesis. Like other triazole fungicides, its main mode of action is the inhibition of cytochrome P450 14α-demethylase (CYP51), a key enzyme in the biosynthesis of sterols such as ergosterol (Vanden Bossche et al., 1990; Zarn et al., 2003). Ergosterol is an essential component of fungal cell membranes, and its disruption compromises fungal viability.
Beyond its antifungal activity, EPX has been shown to interact with endocrine pathways. It acts as an androgen receptor agonist and promotes the synthesis of sex steroid hormones in vitro, which can interfere with developmental processes and individual growth (Kjærstad et al., 2010; Zarn et al., 2003). EPX also showed to be carcinogenic on rats. EPX is therefore considered as a reprotoxic and a suspected carcenogenic (ECHA, 2025a).
The half-life of epoxiconazole is 353.5 days in soil (20°C), 103.4 days in water-sediment (20°C) and 1000 days in water only (20°C) (Lewis et al., 2006), which makes it a very persistant substance in the environment. Its logK\(_{ow}\) above 3 makes it likely to bind to the organic matter in soil. Overall, there is broad agreement in that this substance is Persistent, Bioaccumulative and Toxic (PBT) (ECHA, 2025b).
On earthworms, epoxiconazole impacts growth, maturation and reproduction (Bart, 2019; Bart et al., 2020). In field studies, it was shown to reduce the species diversity, anecic abundance and total biomass (Amossé et al., 2020).

2.2.3 Imidacloprid (IMD)
Imidacloprid (IMD) is a systemic insecticide belonging to the chloronicotinyl (neonicotinoid) family. It is widely used in agriculture across the globe to control sap-feeding insects such as plant hoppers, aphids, termites, Colorado potato beetles, fleas, white grubs, craneflies, crickets, and ants (Lewis et al., 2006). Its applications included lawns and turf, as well as crops such as rice, cereals, maize, potatoes, and sugar beet. It was also used in veterinary medicine, notably in flea treatments for domestic pets. Imidacloprid was commercialized by Bayer in 1991 (Lewis et al., 2006).
In France, the use of neonicotinoids — including imidacloprid — was progressively restricted following the adoption of the 2016 law on the “reconquest of biodiversity, nature and landscapes” (loi pour la reconquête de la biodiversité, de la nature et des paysages). The European Union withdrew the market authorization for imidacloprid in 2020. Currently, only acetamiprid remains approved for use in France and the EU, primarily for veterinary purposes. A temporary derogation had allowed the use of imidacloprid and thiamethoxam for aphid-infested beet crops, but this exemption was definitively revoked in January 2023, reinforcing the ban on neonicotinoids following multiple regulatory actions at both French and European levels (Anses, 2020).
Imidacloprid exerts its toxic effects by acting as an agonist of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), leading to overstimulation and subsequent disruption of the central nervous system in target invertebrates (Chen et al., 2021; Lewis et al., 2006). This mechanism makes it highly effective at low concentrations, but also raises concerns about its non-target effects, particularly on soil invertebrates such as earthworms.
Imidacloprid is also under assessment for endocrine disrupting (ECHA, 2025b).
The half-life of imidacloprid is 2.3 years in fresh water (12°C), 1.1 years in freshwater-sediment (12°C) and 1.4 years in soil (12°C) (Lewis et al., 2006), which makes it a very persistant substance in the environment.
On earthworms, imidacloprid significatively impacts survival but also growth, maturation and reproduction (Dittbrenner et al., 2011; Pelosi et al., 2016; Van Loon et al., 2022). It was also shown to disturbe activities of carboxylesterase (CarE) and glutathione-S- transferases (GST) (Wang et al., 2019). More importantly, it affects earthworms’ burrowing activity, essential for the various ecosystem functions endorsed by earthworms (Capowiez et al., 2006; Dittbrenner et al., 2010).

2.2.4 Environmental concentrations
Recent monitoring data from French agricultural soils reveal substantial variability in pesticide residue levels. Froger et al. (2023) reported imidacloprid concentrations with median values of 2.9 ng/g (0.0029 mg/kg), reaching maximum concentrations of 13.8 ng/g (0.0138 mg/kg) and third quartile values of 5.8 ng/g (0.0058 mg/kg). Epoxiconazole concentrations were higher, with median concentrations of 5.8 ng/g (0.0058 mg/kg), maximum values of 23.6 ng/g (0.0236 mg/kg), and third quartile concentrations of 10.9 ng/g (0.0109 mg/kg). More comprehensive surveys focusing on conventional cereal farming systems show elevated contamination levels (Pelosi et al., 2021). Imidacloprid median concentrations reached 15.1 ng/g (0.0151 mg/kg) with maximum values of 160 ng/g (0.16 mg/kg), while epoxiconazole showed median concentrations of 34.6 ng/g (0.0346 mg/kg) with maximum values of 283 ng/g (0.283 mg/kg). These concentrations can be contextualized against recommended application doses of 168 ng/g for imidacloprid and 153 ng/g for epoxiconazole (Pelosi et al., 2021). Environmental residue levels show that soil contamination can reach substantial fractions of recommended doses, with maximum detected concentrations representing 95% (160/168) of the recommended dose for imidacloprid and 185% (283/153) for epoxiconazole. Median concentrations in conventional cereal farming represent 9% and 23% of recommended doses for imidacloprid and epoxiconazole, respectively.

title: 3  DENS experiment - Impact of density and food quantity
text:
3.1.1 Earthworms and soil
Earthworms used in the original experiment of this study originated from a laboratory culture established from individuals collected between late 2023 and early 2024 in a permanent grassland located in Versailles (48°48′ N, 2°5′ E). The site has been free of pesticide applications for over three decades. Specimens were identified under a binocular microscope following standard taxonomic keys. The culture was maintained at 18 °C in 1 L vessels, with groups of five individuals per vessel. The rearing substrate consisted of loamy soil sampled from the same meadow and identical to that used in Bart (2019) and Bart et al. (2020), according to the texture classification of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), to reproduce conditions close to those of the native habitat. The soil contained 3.26% organic matter (dry weight basis; see Supplementary Information Table S1.1 for soil characteristics). Soil was collected from the 0-20 cm layer, air-dried, and sieved to < 2 mm. Moisture was maintained at 60-70% of the soil’s water-holding capacity (WHC). Earthworms were fed monthly with approximately 6 g (dry weight) of horse dung per group of five individuals, adjusted to 60–80% WHC. The dung was collected long after any veterinary deworming treatment, frozen and thawed twice, and then ground to < 1 mm following the procedure of Lowe & Butt (2005). As recommended by Bart (2018), ten field-collected individuals were barcoded to verify lineage composition; results indicated two genetic lineages within A. caliginosa. To limit potential age-related variation in reproductive performance Hartenstein et al. (1979), individuals used in each reproduction test were less than two months apart in age.
To obtain age-synchronized cohorts, cocoons were retrieved from the breeding containers and then incubated at 18 °C in Petri dishes lined with moistened filter paper. Newly hatched juveniles were collected daily and transferred to soil stored at 4 °C to slow down their development until the start of the experiment. This procedure ensured that all hatchlings were at a comparable developmental stage at the experiment’s onset and allowed for random assignment of individuals to experimental groups.


3.1.2 Population density experiment
To assess the effect of density on earthworm growth and reproduction from the newly hatched juvenile stage to the adult stage, four cosm densities were tested: 1, 2, 5, and 7 individuals per cosm, each in four replicates (hereafter D1, D2, D5, and D7). An additional treatment (D2b) was included to evaluate the effect of food availability independently of density. For each replicate, the corresponding number of earthworms was placed in a cosm consisting of a plastic vessel (11 × 7.7 × 4.5 cm) containing the equivalent of 200 g dry soil humidified at WHC 70%. All cosms were maintained at 18 °C. Each cosm received the equivalent of 3 g of dry horse dung humidified at WHC 70% as food every 14 days, which corresponds to ad libitum conditions for a single earthworm (D1). In the D2b condition, this amount was doubled (6 g every 14 days). Soil was renewed every 28 days. Earthworms were weighed every 14 days, and soil moisture was checked and adjusted weekly. Once earthworms reached adulthood, cocoons were collected every 28 days during soil renewal by wet-sieving the soil through a 1-mm mesh, following Bart et al. (2018).
Statistical analyses were performed to evaluate the effect of population density on juvenile growth and reproductive output. Initial body mass was first compared among density treatments to verify the homogeneity of individuals at the beginning of the experiment. Individual juvenile growth rates were then estimated. Individual juvenile growth rates were then estimated using a linear regression on the weight (\(W\)) through an allometric relationship with a 1/3 power scaling (Gollot et al., 2025). For each individual, a linear regression of structural length against time was then fitted, and the slope of this regression was used as an individual estimate of juvenile growth rate. The effect of population density on juvenile growth rate was tested using a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), with density treatment as a fixed factor. When a significant density effect was detected, pairwise comparisons between density treatments were performed using Tukey post hoc test. Reproductive output was analysed at the replicate level and compared among density treatments using the same statistical framework. Pairwise comparisons between the remaining density treatments were performed using Tukey post hoc tests.

3.3.1 Juvenile growth rate

f_GrowthRate <- function(data){
 
  df_GrowthRate <- data.frame() 
 
  for (i in unique(data$ID_cosm)){

    data_i <- subset(data, ID_cosm == i) 
    Nb_vdt_i <- unique(subset(data_i, t==0)$Nb_vdt)
    Food_i <- unique(subset(data_i, t==0)$Food)
    Nb_rep_i <- unique(subset(data_i, t==0)$Nb_rep)
    Lot_i <- unique(subset(data_i, t==0)$Lot)
    Condition_i <- unique(subset(data_i, t==0)$Condition)
   
    if (length(na.omit(data_i$L))<2) {
      a.Est <- NA
      
    }else if(length(na.omit(data_i$L))==2){ 
     
      a.Est <- (subset(data_i, !t==0)$L - subset(data_i, t==0)$L)/subset(data_i, !t==0)$t # (L(t=t)-L(t=0))/t
     
    }else{
      lm_i <- lm(L~t, data=data_i)
      a.Est <- lm_i$coefficients[2]
    }
   
    df_GrowthRate_i <- data.frame(
      ID_cosm = i,
      Nb_vdt = Nb_vdt_i,
      Food = Food_i,
      Nb_rep = Nb_rep_i,
      Lot = Lot_i,
      Condition = Condition_i,
      Growth_rate = a.Est
    )
    
    df_GrowthRate <- rbind(df_GrowthRate, df_GrowthRate_i)
  }
 
  return(df_GrowthRate) 
}

Figure 3.9: Comparison of growth curves and cumulative reproduction of earthworms under standard (D2, grey) and increased food supply (D2b, blue) at constant density. Small points correspond to the mean weight of earthworm at the replicate level, bigger plain squares correspond to the mean weight at the condition level.





A total of 516 body-mass measurements and 64 reproduction measurements were collected over the 154-day monitoring period. Initial body mass was homogeneous across treatments (median = 10.4 mg, Q1 = 8.7 mg, Q3 = 11.7 mg). Growth rates of each individual were estimated using a linear regression on the structural length of the earthworm (\(L=W^{1/3}\)) which is related to the weight (\(W\)) through an allometric relationship with a 1/3 power scaling (Gollot et al., 2025). A significant effect of density on juvenile growth rate was detected (ANOVA, \(p\) = 0.02). However, post hoc comparisons (Tukey test) revealed that only the contrast between the two extremes of population densities was statistically significant (densities of 1 vs. 7 individuals per cosm, \(p\) = 0.016). No individual reached maturity at the highest population density and we were not able to keep population density constant due to mortality. As a result we excluded this treatment from the statistical analysis of reproduction data. A possible decrease in reproduction with population density was detected (-43% between density 2 and density 5) with high inter-replicate variability (Tukey test : \(p\) = 0.051, Figure 1).
At the highest density (D7), one individual died in each replicate at different times (days 14, 28, 56, 70, and 84 depending on the replicate). The remaining individuals (\(n\) = 6 per replicate) survived until the end of the experiment (154 days). These replicates were excluded from the main analysis due to uncertainty regarding the exact timing of mortality.
Only two replicates yielded reproduction data in the D2b condition (density 2 with increased food supply), and these displayed contrasting dynamics. One replicate was monitored until day 154, whereas the second stopped at day 84, resulting in a visible discontinuity in cumulative reproduction after this time point. Prior to day 84, increasing food availability at constant density (D2b) resulted in only limited decreases in growth and similar reproduction compared with D2.
Overall, both growth and reproduction tends to decrease with increasing density.

title: 4  Synthesis of available data
text:
4.1 Data obtained during Sylvain Bart PhD
A significant part of the data are from the PhD of Sylvain Bart (Bart, 2018).
The first part of the data are from its article on Aporrectodea caliginosa life-cycle (Bart, 2019) where he studied the impact of food and density on growth and reproduction. The second part comes from the study of the impact of the Swing Gold pesticide on growth and reproduction (Bart et al., 2020). The control data from this study can be used to inform a DEB model.

title: 4  Synthesis of available data
text:
4.1.1 Earthworms, soil and food used in all Sylvain Bart experiments
Earthworm culture (Bart, 2019) :

Origin of the first earthworms : Adults of Aporrectodea caliginosa s.s. from an agriculture field at INRA (Estrées-mons, 49°52′ N 3°01′E) (refered later as the Mons culture)
Earthworms are cultured in a climate room at 15 ± 1 °C
Soil : a Luvisol (FAO soil classification), sampled from the top 0–20 cm in a permanent meadow in Versailles (48°48′ N, 2°5′ E) (refered later as Closeaux soil).
Food : horse dung which was frozen and defrosted twice and then milled (< 1 mm) as presented in Lowe and Butt (2005).



4.1.2 Experiments from Bart (2019)

Soil : Renewed every 28 days and maintained at 70% of the water holding capacity (WHC) (corresponding to 28% of water content).
Food : The horse dung at 70% of the water holding capacity and mixed with the soil.
Vessels : 1 L plastic vessels with 400 g equivalent dry soil.
Temperature : 15 ± 1 °C
Growth measurements every 14 days until they reached 500 g and then every 7 days to monitor the switch to adult stage


4.1.2.1 Experiment 1
Monitoring of the growth of 10 earthworms under ad libitum condition : 3 g/ind/14 days of horse dung milled at < 1mm. Earthworms are individually placed in a 1 L vessel.
This experiment can be separated in 2 experiments :

XP1_1 (Figure 4.1) : The growth of earthworms individually placed in 1L vessels. These earthworms could not reproduce when adult.
XP1_2 (Figure 4.2) : The growth of adult earthworms pooled first by 2 for 84 days (3 vessels with 2 individuals, for each food condition), then by 3 for 84 days (2 vessels with 3 individuals, for each food condition), and finally by 6 (all in- dividuals in one vessel, for each food condition) for 84 days. (corresponding to the first part of experiment 6 in Bart (2019)).

title: 4  Synthesis of available data
text:
4.3 Usefull data from litterature
An estimate of cocoon energy content was required to parameterize the reproduction in the DEB model for A. caliginosa. Direct measurements of cocoon energy density are not available for this species. We therefore relied on published calorimetric data for Lumbricidae reported by Cumminns & Wuycheck (1971), who measured the energy density of whole individuals (“entire animals of various stages”). Mean energy densities were 5,690 cal g⁻¹ dry weight (n = 3), corresponding to 19,098 J g-1 dry weight, and 782 cal g-1 wet weight (n = 1), corresponding to 3,268 J g-1 wet weight. Although these measurements were not performed on cocoons specifically, they provide an order-of-magnitude estimate for annelid biomass energy density. Assuming a mean cocoon fresh mass of 10 mg, this corresponds to an energy content of approximately 33 J per cocoon (based on wet weight energy density). Comparable energy densities have been reported for soil invertebrates in other calorimetric studies (e.g. Driver et al. (1974), Eggleton & Schramm (2004)), supporting the use of this approximation for the model prior on the energy of an egg.

title: 5  Model formulation
text:
5.1 Classication DEB standard formulation
Reserve energy dynamic
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm d t} = \frac{\{\dot p_{Am}\}_t}{L} \ \left(f - \frac{E\ \nu_t}{\{\dot p_{Am}\}_t}\right)
\]
With :
Growth
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm d L}{\mathrm d t} &= \frac{\nu_t}{3\ (\frac{E}{E_m} + g)} \left(\frac{E}{E_m} - \frac{L}{L_m}\right) \\ \\
K_m &= \frac{[\dot p_{M,t}]}{[E_G]} \\
E_m &= \frac{\{\dot p_{Am}\}_t}{\nu_t}\\
g &= \frac{[E_G]}{\kappa_{\text{real}}\ E_m}\\
L_m &= \frac{\nu_t}{K_m\ g}
\end{aligned}
\]
With :
\[
W_W = L^3 \left(1+\frac{E}{E_m}w\right)
\]
With :
Maturity and reproduction
\[
\dot p_C = \frac{g\ E}{g + \frac{E}{E_m}} (\nu_t\ L^2 + K_m\ L^3)
\]
With :
\[
\dot p_R = (1-\kappa_{\text{real}})\ \dot p_C - \dot k_{J,t}\ E_h
\]
With :
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}E_H}{\mathrm{d}t}=
\begin{cases}
E_H \leq E_H^p,\ & \dot{p}_R\\
E_H > E_H^p,\ & 0
\end{cases}
\]
With :
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}t}=
\begin{cases}
E_H \leq E_H^p,\ & 0 \\
E_H > E_H^p,\ & \kappa_R\ \frac{\dot{p}_R}{E_{0}}
\end{cases}
\]
With :
Effect of temperature on rates
\[
\begin{aligned}
s_A &= \exp(\frac{T_A}{T_{ref}-\frac{T_A}{T_{exp}+273.15}})\\
s_{rH} &= \frac{1 + \exp (\frac{T_A^H}{T^H}-\frac{T_A^H}{T_{ref}+ 273.15})}{1 + \exp (\frac{T_A^H}{T^H}-\frac{T_A^H}{T_{exp}+273.15})}\\
T_c &= s_A (T_{exp}+273.15 \geq T_{ref}) s_{rH} + (T_{exp} + 273.15 < T_{ref})\\ \\
\{\dot p_{Am}\}_t &= \{\dot p_{Am}\}\ T_c\\
[\dot p_{M,t}] &= [\dot p_{M}]\ T_c \\
\nu_t &= \nu \ T_c \\
\dot k_{J,t} &= \dot k_{J} \ T_c
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 5  Model formulation
text:
\(E\) : Energy in the reserve (\(J\))
\(\nu_t\) : Energy conductance at temperature \(T_{exp}\) (\(cm.d^{-1}\))





\(L\) : Structural volumetric length (\(cm\))
\([\dot p_{M,t}]\) : Volume-specific maintenance rate (\(J.d^{-1}.cm^{-3}\))
\([E_G]\) : Volume-specific cost for structure (\(J.cm^{-3}\))




\(W_W\) : Wet weight of the earthworm (\(g\))
\(w\) : Contribution of reserve to body weight (\(g.cm^{-3}\))





\(\dot p_C\) : Mobilized energy flux from reserve (\(J.d^{-1}\))




\(\dot p_R\) : Allocated energy flux to reproduction (\(J.d^{-1}\))
\(\dot k_{J,t}\) : Maturity maintenance rate (\(d^{-1}\))




\(E_h\) : Maturity (\(J\))
\(E_h^p\) : Maturity at puberty (\(J\))




\(R\) : Cumulated reproduction (#)
\(\kappa_R\) : Reproduction efficiency (-)
\(E_0\) : Energy cost for an egg (\(J\))

title: 5  Model formulation
text:
5.2 Tested model formulations
Our model formulation is based on the standard DEB model (Kooijman, 2009), using the extended model developed by Gergs et al. (2022) as a starting point. Model notation and terminology follow the conventions defined in standard DEB theory (Kooijman, 2009). The standard DEB model describes four primary state variables at the individual level of the earthworm : (i) Structural length, \(L\); (ii) Energy of the reserve, \(E\); (iii) Maturity, \(E_h\); and (iv) Reproduction, \(R\), corresponding to the cumulated number of offspring produced by the individual. Environmental state variables are also taken into account as inputs (temperature, organic matter content). Model parameters are detailed in Table 5.1, while state and intermediate variables are listed in Supplementary Information Table 5.2.
Several alternative model formulations were evaluated to test key biological assumptions.
Our primary objective was to mechanistically link the quantity and quality of available organic matter to the functional response (\(f\)). Organic matter from soil and horse dung were treated separately due to differences in quality and bioavailability. Horse dung was assumed to contain 90% organic matter with an energy density of 3100 kcal/kg (13 000 J/g, \(\mu_{OM}\)) (Chastain, 2022; Sahu et al., 2016). In contrast, soil organic matter was assumed to provide less usable energy. To account for this difference, a scaling factor (\(r_{OM}\)) was introduced to relate the energy content of soil organic matter to that of horse dung.
The ingestion rate was formulated as a function of the maximum surface-area-specific searching rate, \(\{\dot{F}_m\}\), or the maximum mass-specific searching rate, \([\dot{F}_m]\), individual size, organic matter availability, and population density (Equation 5.1).
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot Q_{matter} &= \{\dot{F}_m\}\ L^2  &(\text{version L}) \\
\dot Q_{matter} &= [\dot{F}_m]\ d_V L^3 &(\text{version W})
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.1}\]
To prevent the ingestion of a quantity of soil greater than that corresponding to the maximum energy absorbable by a worm per day (\(\dot Q_{f,max}\)), \(\dot Q_{matter}\) is capped at the soil quantity \(\dot Q_{matter,max}\) equivalent to this energy threshold (Equation 5.2).
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot Q_{f,max} &= \frac{\{\dot p_{Am}\}_T \ L^2}{\kappa_X} \\
\dot Q_{matter,max} &= \frac{\dot Q_{f,max}\ W_{cosm}}{(OM_{horse} + OM_{soil}\ r_{OM})\ \mu_{OM}}\\ \\
\dot Q_{matter,real} &= \min(\dot Q_{matter}, \dot Q_{matter,max})
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.2}\]
with :

\(\{\dot p_{Am}\}_T\), the temperature-corrected surface-specific maximum assimilation rate (J\(\cdot\)d\(^{-1} \cdot\)cm\(^{-2}\))
\(\kappa_X\), the digestion efficiency
\(W_{cosm}\), the dry mass of matter in the cosm (g)
\(OM_{horse}\) and \(OM_{soil}\) the dry mass of organic matter from horse dung and soil in the cosm, respectively (g).

The ingested energy then depends on the quantities of soil and organic matter in the cosm and their respective energetic contributions (Equation 5.3).
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot Q_{f}^{soil} &= \dot Q_{matter,real} \times \frac{OM_{soil}}{W_{cosm}} \times \mu_{OM}\ r_{OM}\\
\dot Q_{f}^{horse} &= \dot Q_{matter,real} \times \frac{OM_{horse}}{W_{cosm}} \times \mu_{OM} \\ \\
\dot Q_{f}^{tot} &= \dot Q_{f}^{horse} + \dot Q_{f}^{soil}
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.3}\]
with :

\(\dot Q_{f}^{soil}\), the amount of energy ingested by an earthworm from soil organic matter per day (J/d)
\(\dot Q_{f}^{horse}\), the amount of energy consumed by an earthworm from the horse dung organic matter per day (J/d)
\(\dot Q_{f}^{tot}\) sums the two previous quantities

Consumption by individuals was explicitly incorporated into the temporal dynamics of organic matter in the cosm with the calculation of the rates of consumption of horse dung and soil organic matter (\(\dot{OM}_{out}^{horse}\) and \(\dot{OM}_{out}^{soil}\) in \(\mathrm{g_{OM}.d^{-1}}\)) depending on the number of individuals in the cosm (\(n_{ind}\)) (Equation 5.5). If the available organic matter is insufficient to cover the requirements of all individuals, the quantity is distributed equally among them.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm d OM_{soil}}{\mathrm d t} &= -\frac{\dot Q_{f}^{soil}}{\mu_{OM}\ r_{OM}}\ Nb_{ind}\\
\frac{\mathrm d OM_{horse}}{\mathrm d t} &= -\frac{\dot Q_{f}^{horse}}{\mu_{OM}}\ Nb_{ind}
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.4}\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm d OM_{soil}}{\mathrm d t} &= -\frac{\dot Q_{f}^{soil}}{\mu_{OM}\ r_{OM}}\ n_{ind}\\
\frac{\mathrm d OM_{horse}}{\mathrm d t} &= -\frac{\dot Q_{f}^{horse}}{\mu_{OM}}\ n_{ind}
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.5}\]
The functional response (\(f\)) was derived as a saturating function of the ratio between ingested energy and maximal ingestion capacity. Within the DEB framework, \(f\) represents the degree to which food availability limits assimilation, ranging from food limitation (\(f \approx 0\)) to ad libitum conditions (\(f \approx 1\)). A saturating relationship was therefore used to reflect the progressive increase in assimilated energy as ingestion approaches the maximal capacity of the organism. Two alternative formulations were tested (Equation 5.6): (i) a classical hyperbolic response, commonly used in DEB applications, in which \(f = 0.5\) when ingested energy reaches half of its maximum value, and (ii) a normalized hyperbolic formulation constraining \(f\) between 0 and 1 such that \(f = 1\) when ingestion reaches its maximal value. This formulation allows maximal ingestion to correspond biologically to ad libitum feeding conditions, where additional food no longer increases assimilation and life-history performance.
\[
\begin{aligned}
f &= \frac{X}{1+X} &\text{with }\  X &= \frac{\dot Q_{f,tot}}{\frac 1 2 \dot Q_{f,max}} &\text{(version Y)} \\
f &= \frac{X}{K\ (1-X)+X} &\text{with }\  X &= \frac{\dot Q_{f,tot}}{\dot Q_{f,max}} &\text{(version K)}
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.6}\]
Reserve mobilization, growth, maturation, and reproduction follow standard DEB equations with temperature correction. A baseline formulation assuming a fixed allocation fraction throughout the life cycle was considered (equation version F), consistent with the standard DEB \(\kappa\)-rule. In addition, we introduced a model variant with a context-dependent allocation rule for \(\kappa\) to account for reproductive opportunities (equation version C, Equation 5.7). Specifically, energy allocation shifts when individuals reach maturity (at time \(t_p\)), reflecting the biological constraint that reproduction requires the presence of conspecifics. This transition can occur progressively over a characteristic timescale \(\tau\) (d).
\[
\begin{aligned}
x &=
\begin{cases}
\text{if } E_h < E_h^p, & 0 \\
\text{if } E_h \geq E_h^p, & \min \left( 1, \frac{t-t_p}{\tau}\right)
\end{cases} \\
\kappa_{real} &= (1-x)\kappa_J + x\ \kappa_A
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.7}\]
Finally, two alternative formulations were considered to relate structural size (\(L\)) to fresh body mass (\(W_W\)), reflecting different assumptions regarding reserve (\(E\)) contribution to total body weight. In the first formulation, reserve contribution was assumed proportional to structural size, consistent with the weak homeostasis assumption of DEB theory, whereby reserve covaries with structure. In the second formulation, reserve contribution was represented independently of structural size, allowing fresh body mass to vary according to reserve dynamics independently of structural growth (Equation 5.8).
\[
\begin{aligned}
W_W &= L^3 \left( d_V + \frac{E}{E_m} w_E \right) & \text{(version w)} \\
W_W &= L^3 \ d_V + E\ d_E  & \text{(version e)}
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.8}\]
with :

\(d_V\) the density of structure (g\(\cdot\)cm\(^{-3}\))
\(d_E\) the density of reserve (g\(\cdot\)J\(^{-1}\))
\(w_E\) the contribution of reserve to body weight (g\(\cdot\)cm\(^{-3}\))
\(E_m\) the maximum reserve (J).

Models are designated with a combination of letters corresponding to the different variants of equations.

5.3 Model parametrization and calibration
The DEB model was calibrated and evaluated using both literature datasets and the new density experiment conducted in this study. Together, these datasets cover multiple life stages and experimental conditions, including isolated individuals, grouped adults, and juveniles reared under different density and food availability conditions. The main characteristics of each dataset, including density treatment and feeding conditions are summarized in Table 5.3 (more detail Chapter 4). This combination of datasets provides complementary information for characterizing growth, maturation, and reproduction processes across a range of environmental conditions (temperature, feeding, population density).

The DEB models were calibrated and evaluated using both literature datasets and the new density experiment conducted in this study. Together, these datasets cover multiple life stages and experimental conditions, including isolated individuals, grouped adults, and juveniles reared under different density and food availability conditions. The main characteristics of each dataset, including density treatment and feeding conditions are summarized in Table 5.3. This combination of datasets provides complementary information for characterizing growth, maturation, and reproduction processes across a range of environmental conditions (temperature, feeding, population density).
Model calibration was performed exclusively using datasets corresponding to juvenile individuals and adults maintained in groups. Data from isolated adults were excluded from the calibration procedure because reproduction cannot occur in the absence of mating partners, potentially affecting energy allocation patterns and biasing the estimation of reproductive parameters.
Model parameters were estimated within a Bayesian framework using largely weakly informative priors, while incorporating more constrained priors for parameters with available biological or physiological knowledge. The full set of prior distributions is detailed in Chapter 6 The models were implemented in the MCSim environment. Parameter inference was performed using Bayesian numerical calibration following Bois (2009). Likelihood functions were defined assuming normally distributed errors for body weight and Poisson-distributed counts for reproduction. Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulations were run with 3 chains for 30,000 iterations to approximate posterior distributions of model parameters which were estimated from the last 10,000 iterations of the MCMC chains. Point estimates were defined as the modes of the posterior distributions with their 95% credibility intervals.
Not all possible combinations of model assumptions were tested in a full factorial design. Candidate formulations were instead evaluated sequentially, based on biological plausibility and on the behaviour of preliminary fits. Eight combinations were retained for comparison: L.Y.F.w, L.Y.F.e, L.K.F.e, W.K.F.e, L.Y.C.e, L.K.C.e, W.Y.C.e, and W.K.C.e. This selection allowed the main alternative assumptions concerning searching-rate scaling, functional-response shape, post-maturation allocation, and reserve contribution to body mass to be compared while limiting redundant or weakly supported formulations. Model comparison was based on the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), which balances goodness-of-fit and model complexity by penalizing models with a higher number of parameters, but also on the RMSE of each experiment. In addition, to investigate whether model performance and prediction bias varied across experimental conditions, predicted-observed relationships were examined according to temperature, density, food availability, and developmental stage.
A global sensitivity analysis was conducted on the best-performing model using the Sobol method with the Jansen estimator, implemented in the “sensitivity” R package (Ioss et al., 2026). Two complementary analyses were performed: one including the parameters governing temperature dependence and one excluding them, in order to distinguish the contribution of thermal correction from that of the remaining physiological and environmental parameters. Parameter values were varied independently within ±10% of their posterior estimates to quantify their relative influence on model outputs.
The sensitivity analysis was based on simulations of the Gollot2026_D2 experiment, in which two earthworms were maintained per cosm under moderate food availability. Body mass, reserve energy, and maturity were evaluated at both the juvenile stage (\(t = 50\) days) and the adult stage (\(t = 140\) days). Reproductive output at \(t = 140\) days and the total amount of organic matter remaining in the cosm at \(t = 50\) days were also included as endpoints. These endpoints were selected to characterize parameter influence on energy acquisition, individual state, life-history transitions, and reproductive performance at contrasting developmental stages.
Finally, the case of isolated adults was therefore explored only through simulations to investigate the resulting patterns of energy allocation in the absence of reproductive opportunities. Two alternative formulations were considered: (i) maintaining the juvenile allocation fraction throughout adulthood (\(\kappa_J\)), and (ii) introducing a transition toward the adult allocation fraction (\(\kappa_A\) ) after maturation, as implemented for grouped adults.

format_summary <- function(df) {
  df %>%
    rename_with(~ str_remove(., "\\.1\\.$")) %>%
    rownames_to_column("stat") %>%
    pivot_longer(
      cols = -c(stat, Model),
      names_to = "param",
      values_to = "value"
    ) %>%
    pivot_wider(
      names_from = stat,
      values_from = value
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      value = str_c(
        round(Result_mode, 3),
        " [", round(`2.5%`, 3),
        " ; ", round(`97.5%`, 3), "]"
      )
    ) %>%
    dplyr::select(Model, param, value) %>%
    pivot_wider(
      names_from = param,
      values_from = value
    )
}

Calibration of all tested model formulations was achieved using three MCMC chains. Convergence diagnostics indicated satisfactory mixing and convergence overall, with chains converging toward similar posterior distributions and Gelman–Rubin statistics close to 1 (\(\hat{R}\)). However, for some model formulations, posterior estimates of specific parameters approached the upper or lower bounds of their biologically constrained priors, suggesting limited parameter identifiability or weak support for these formulations. Model comparison based on BIC revealed substantial differences among formulations (Table 6.1).
Preliminary model comparisons supported the stepwise selection of candidate formulations. Models assuming a fixed allocation rule throughout the life cycle (F) systematically produced poorer fits and overestimated post-maturation growth in grouped adults, whereas formulations including a progressive transition in allocation after maturation (Equation 5.7, C) better reproduced the adult growth plateau. Models using the classical hyperbolic functional response (Equation 5.6, Y) also yielded substantially higher BIC values than those using the normalized formulation (Equation 5.6, K), as predicted assimilation remained insufficient to reproduce observed growth trajectories across experiments. The formulation in which reserve contribution to fresh body mass scaled with structure (L.Y.F.w) was evaluated only once because this assumption was weakly supported by Bart2019_XP3. In this experiment, alternating between soil supplemented with horse dung and soil alone produced only limited changes in fresh body mass, whereas the structure-dependent formulation implied a stronger influence of reserve dynamics on body mass (Equation 5.8, w). Consistently, this formulation performed less well than those assuming that reserve contribution was independent of structural size (Equation 5.8, e). Subsequent comparisons therefore focused mainly on formulations combining a progressive allocation transition (Equation 5.7, C) with reserve independence (Equation 5.8, e), while retaining selected fixed energy allocation (F) formulations as reference models.
The two best-supported models shared three common characteristics: (i) a progressive change in energy allocation after maturation (Equation 5.7, C), (ii) a normalized hyperbolic functional response (Equation 5.6, K), and (iii) a formulation in which reserve contribution to fresh body mass was independent of structural size (Equation 5.8, e). The only difference between these two formulations concerned the scaling of the maximum searching rate, which was either structural-mass-specific (Equation 5.3, W) or surface-area-specific (Equation 5.3, L) : model W.K.C.e (BIC = 92.2) and model L.K.C.e (BIC = 46.0). whereas all other formulations had considerably higher BIC values (99-551).
Models assuming a fixed allocation rule throughout the life cycle (F) systematically resulted in poorer fits. Similarly, models using the classical hyperbolic formulation for the functional response (Y) showed much higher BIC values than those using the normalized formulation (K). In practice, these formulations systematically failed to reproduce observed growth trajectories, with predicted assimilation remaining insufficient to sustain realistic growth across experiments. Models assuming reserve contribution proportional to structure (w) also performed less well than formulations assuming reserve independence (e) (see Supplementary information Section S2).
Although the two best models had substantially different BIC values (\(\Delta\)BIC = 46.2), both provided qualitatively similar predictions for most datasets. However, they greatly differed for the key experiment Bart2019_XP3, where earthworms were alternately fed with soil only and soil supplemented with horse dung. The model with a structural-mass-specific maximum searching rate (W.K.C.e) reproduced the observed growth trajectory more accurately during the final phase of the experiment.This difference was reflected by a lower weight RMSE for the W.K.C.e compared with L.K.C.e (0.035 vs. 0.071, respectively). Consequently, despite a higher overall BIC, W.K.C.e was retained for subsequent analyses because it provided a substantially better fit for Bart2019_XP3 while producing similar fits for the other experiments (Figure 6.61 & fig-pred_F_CLKe).
Parameter estimates for the retained model are presented in Table 5.1. Parameter values were generally consistent between W.K.C.e and L.K.C.e, with as expected, the main differences concerning the ingestion-related parameters \([\dot{F}_m]\), \(\{\dot{F}_m\}\) and \(K\). For both formulations, posterior estimates of the maximum searching rate approached the upper bound of the prior distribution.
Although the retained model adequately reproduced the main growth and reproduction trajectories across experiments (W.K.C.e, Figure 6.61), some condition-specific deviations remained. For body mass, grouped individuals under low-food conditions (Bart2019_XP4_2) showed an overestimation of the adult plateau, whereas the adult plateau was well estimated for grouped individuals under high-food conditions (Bart2019_XP1_2). This pattern was also observed with the L.K.C.e model. In the density experiments at densities 2 and 5 (Gollot2026_D2 and Gollot2026_D5), the transition between juvenile growth and the adult plateau remained more abrupt in simulations than in observations, despite the introduction of a progressive allocation transition over the timescale parameter (\(\tau\)). In contrast, this transition was more accurately reproduced for individuals at density 2 with increased food supply (Gollot2026_D2b).
For reproduction, the main deviations also corresponded to specific experimental conditions rather than to a general model bias. For grouped individuals under low-food conditions (Bart2019_XP4_2), observed reproduction decreased when density increased from three to six individuals per cosm, whereas the model predicted similar reproductive outputs between the two conditions. Reproduction was also slightly underestimated for grouped individuals at high-food conditions (Bart2019_XP1_2). For individuals at density 2 with increased food supply (Gollot2026_D2b), reproductive output was overestimated, with observed reproduction remaining substantially lower than predicted by the model.

f_Quality_fit <- function(df, group){
  df_res <- df |> 
    group_by(across(all_of(group))) |> 
    summarise(
        Fold_mean = mean(Fold, na.rm = TRUE),
        Bias = mean(Residuals, na.rm = TRUE),
        Mean_relative_error = mean(Relative_error, na.rm = TRUE),
        Mean_LogPredObs = mean(LogPredObs, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
      ) |> 
    ungroup() |> 
    mutate(Mean_PredObs = exp(Mean_LogPredObs))
}

The predicted-observed analysis was used to explore whether model fit showed consistent trends with temperature and density. These comparisons remain descriptive because the experimental factors were not orthogonal, particularly density and per-capita food availability.
For body mass, fit quality was similar at 15 and 18 °C, with no clear temperature-specific bias. Across density treatments, fit quality varied without a strictly monotonic pattern, although the largest deviations were observed for juveniles at density 7, where body mass tended to be overestimated. Adult body mass was generally reproduced with limited bias across density conditions.
For reproduction, no general temperature-related pattern was identified, as the larger residuals at 18°C were mainly driven by specific experiments. Likewise, variation across density treatments was strongly experiment-dependent, with both over- and underestimation depending on the condition.c

The global sensitivity analysis revealed that model outputs were strongly influenced by the parameters governing temperature correction when these were included in the analysis. Because \(T_{\mathrm{ref}}\) is an arbitrary reference value used in the thermal correction, its high sensitivity was not interpreted biologically. Among the biologically meaningful thermal parameters, \(T_H\) contributed substantially to body mass, reserve energy, reproduction, and organic matter dynamics. Maturity-related endpoints remained primarily controlled by the juvenile allocation fraction (\(\kappa_J\)), with additional contributions from thermal correction parameters. Differences between first-order and total-order indices indicated substantial interactions between temperature correction, energy allocation, and other physiological processes.
When temperature-related parameters were excluded, sensitivity patterns became more process-specific. Body mass, maturity, and reproduction were mainly governed by \(\kappa_J\), with juvenile body mass also influenced by \(E_G\), \(\{\dot{p}_{Am}\}\), \(d_V\), and the ratio between \(\{\dot{p}_{Am}\}\) and \([\dot{p}_{M}]\). Reserve energy was primarily influenced by the energy conductance (\(v\)) and the surface-specific maximum assimilation rate (\(\{\dot{p}_{Am}\}\)). Total organic matter remaining in the cosm was mainly influenced by \(\kappa_J\), followed by \(\{\dot{p}_{Am}\}\), \(E_G\), and, to a lesser extent, \([\dot{F}_m]\), atio between \(\{\dot{p}_{Am}\}\) and \([\dot{p}_{M}]\), and \(d_V\). Overall, these results highlight the central role of energy allocation in life-history predictions, while environmental resource dynamics depend on a broader combination of allocation, assimilation, growth, and food-acquisition processes.
