Figure 7.2: Predicted Reproduction for each experiment.





The formulation maintaining the juvenile allocation fraction throughout adulthood (\(\kappa_J\)) reproduced the observed growth trajectories of isolated adults more accurately than the formulation including a transition toward the adult allocation fraction (\(\kappa_A\)), which systematically underestimated growth after maturation (Figure 7.1). This result suggests that isolated adults maintain growth patterns closer to those of juveniles than to those of grouped reproducing adults.
However, despite the absence of observed cocoon production in isolated adults, both formulations still predicted a non-zero allocation of energy toward reproduction after maturation (Figure 7.2). This discrepancy indicates that the energetic fate of the reproductive flux remains inadequately represented in the current model formulations and must be further investigated.

title: 8  Discussion & Conclusion
text:
8.1 Resource sharing and apparent density effects on growth and reproduction
The present study combined literature datasets and new density-dependent experiments to develop a mechanistic DEB model for A. caliginosa linking growth, maturation, and reproduction to food availability and population density. By extending previous experiments to the juvenile stage under different density conditions, this work provides new insights into the mechanisms underlying density dependence in earthworms and their representation within a DEB framework.
The density experiment confirmed that increasing the number of individuals per cosm reduced juvenile growth, adult body mass, and reproductive output. However, because all microcosms received the same total amount of food irrespective of the number of individuals, increasing density simultaneously reduced food availability per individual. Under these experimental conditions, the observed reduction in performance therefore reflects primarily a resource-sharing effect rather than density dependence sensu stricto.
Consistent with this interpretation, the DEB model reproduced juvenile growth without an explicit density-dependent process, as treatment differences emerged from variation in per-capita access to organic matter. Model simulations further supported this interpretation, showing lower food availability and functional response at higher densities (Figure 6.66), and indicating that differences in resource acquisition explained much of the variation in growth and maturation among treatments. The predicted-observed analysis did not reveal a monotonic decline in fit quality with density. However, the largest deviations were observed at the highest juvenile density (D7), where body mass tended to be overestimated. This discrepancy may reflect the assumption of homogeneous individuals and equal resource sharing within each cosm. In every D7 replicate, one individual remained consistently smaller than the others and eventually died, thereby lowering the observed mean body mass relative to the homogeneous trajectory predicted by the model. This suggests that, under high-density conditions, individual heterogeneity and asymmetric access to resources may become important, even though resource sharing explains the overall density-related pattern.
This result differs somewhat from previous earthworm studies that reported density-dependent effects even under apparently non-limiting food conditions. For example, Klok (2007) observed delayed maturation and reduced cocoon production at high densities despite surplus food availability and interpreted these effects as reduced ingestion caused by spatial interference among individuals. Similarly, Rakel et al. (2020) reproduced density-related reductions in growth in E. fetida through crowding effects affecting food acquisition. In contrast, the present results indicate that much of the variation observed here can be explained without invoking an explicit crowding effect, suggesting that reduced access to food was the dominant mechanism under our experimental conditions.
The comparison between D2 and D2b provides additional support for this interpretation. Doubling food input at density 2 produced only limited increases in growth and reproduction despite substantially greater horse dung availability. Model simulations indicate that the functional response in D2 was already close to saturation (\(f \approx 1\)), implying that additional food yielded little energetic benefit. Under these conditions, D2 may already approximate ad libitum feeding, making D2b of limited physiological benefit despite greater food supply. Moreover, because the cosms were renewed every 28 days, the remaining organic matter was periodically removed and reset, particularly reducing the excess organic matter accumulated in D2b. Cosm renewal therefore limited the persistence of differences in resource availability between treatments. Overall, once food acquisition approaches saturation, increasing organic matter input does not necessarily translate into greater assimilation and may instead alter the physical or microbial environment of the cosm. From a practical perspective, these results also suggest that standard feeding conditions similar to D2 may already be sufficient to maintain near-maximal growth and reproduction, while requiring substantially less horse dung.
Although the present design does not allow complete separation of resource-mediated and density-dependent effects, it highlights the importance of explicitly accounting for per-capita food availability when interpreting earthworm density experiments. Future experiments manipulating density while maintaining equivalent per-capita food conditions (e.g., a high-density treatment with ad libitum food availability) would help determine whether crowding effects independent of resource limitation emerge in A. caliginosa.
The density experiments conducted here also improve the estimation of age at maturity compared with previous experimental designs. In Bart et al. (2020), individuals were isolated during the juvenile stage and paired only once adulthood was visually detected. Because maturity checks occurred at discrete time intervals, the true age at maturity may have been overestimated by up to one observation interval. In contrast, earthworms in the present density experiment were maintained in groups from the beginning of the experiment, ensuring continuous reproductive opportunity once maturity was reached. This design removes the observational delay between physiological maturation and effective reproduction and therefore provides more reliable data for calibrating life-history transitions within the DEB model.

title: 8  Discussion & Conclusion
text:
8.2 Energy assimilation and functional response
A major objective of this study was to mechanistically relate the functional response (\(f\)) to the quantity and quality of organic matter available in the environment. Unlike several previous earthworm DEB studies such as Rakel et al. (2020) and Gergs et al. (2022), where the functional response was estimated independently for each experiment, the present model explicitly links assimilated energy to measurable environmental variables, namely the amounts of horse dung and soil organic matter present in the cosm.
The model comparison strongly supported formulations using a normalized hyperbolic function relating ingestion to the functional response. In classical hyperbolic formulations (David et al., 2018; Gergs et al., 2022; Kooijman, 2009), the functional response asymptotically approaches 1 but never reaches it even when ingestion reaches its maximum value. The normalized formulation avoids this inconsistency by constraining the function between 0 and 1 while maintaining a flexible curvature through parameter \(K\).
The results also support a strong difference in energetic quality between horse dung and soil organic matter. The low estimated value of \(r_{OM}\) (0.03) indicates that soil organic matter contributed little to assimilated energy relative to horse dung, consistent with the negligible growth observed under soil-only conditions in Bart2019_XP3 (Figure 6.66). Such low energetic contribution of soil organic matter likely reflects the limited accessibility and digestibility of native soil carbon relative to fresh organic amendments. Differences in biochemical quality and decomposability among organic matter sources are well documented in soils, with fresh organic amendments generally providing more labile and energetically accessible compounds than stabilized soil organic matter (Lorenz et al., 2024).
Nevertheless, quantifying ingestion and assimilation in endogeic earthworms remains particularly difficult because these organisms live directly within their food matrix. Unlike aquatic or surface-feeding organisms, ingestion cannot easily be measured without disturbing the animals and modifying their behaviour. Consequently, most available estimates rely on indirect approaches such as defecation rates, gut transit measurements, or nitrogen assimilation efficiencies. For example, Barley (1959) showed that A. caliginosa may process substantial quantities of soil relative to its body mass, with smaller individuals ingesting proportionally more material than larger ones. Similarly, Whalen & Parmelee (1999) estimated organic matter consumption indirectly from nitrogen assimilation efficiencies, while Taylor & Taylor (2014) used fungal spores as natural tracers to estimate gut transit time and daily egestion rates. Together, these studies illustrate that energy acquisition in earthworms results from multiple interacting processes, including burrowing activity, ingestion, digestion, gut transit, and assimilation efficiency. Consequently, the effective acquisition of assimilable energy may not scale solely with structural surface area.
Experiment Bart2019_XP3 was particularly informative in this regard because earthworms were alternately maintained on soil alone and on soil supplemented with horse dung. This experimental condition generated strong temporal variations in both the quantity and quality of available organic matter, providing a stringent test of how food acquisition should scale with body size under changing feeding conditions. Under these circumstances, the formulation in which the maximum searching rate scaled with structural mass provided a better fit than the formulation based on structural surface area. However, this result should be interpreted cautiously. The estimated value of \([\dot{F}_m]\) reached approximately 4 g\(_{soil}\).d\(^{-1}\).g\(_{worm}^{-1}\), which is far above available estimates of soil processing rates for A. caliginosa. For instance, Barley (1959) reported defecation rates of approximately 0.32 g dry faeces g\(^{-1}\) fresh weight d\(^{-1}\) in small individuals and 0.22 g dry faeces g\(^{-1}\) fresh weight d\(^{-1}\) in larger individuals. Interpreted literally, the estimated $[_m]$$ would therefore imply unrealistically high soil ingestion rates. This discrepancy suggests that \([\dot{F}_m]\) should not be interpreted as a direct measure of ingestion capacity, but rather as an effective parameter compensating for simplified representation of food acquisition and assimilation. In the current formulation, ingestion is assumed to depend on organic matter density in the cosm, but earthworms may selectively ingest organic-rich microsites, mucus-enriched soil, microbial biomass, or partially decomposed dung particles rather than processing soil homogenously. In addition, the energetic value of horse dung was fixed, although its actual assimilable energy may vary with decomposition state and microbial activity.
Compared with Gergs et al. (2022), the present model yielded markedly different parameter estimates, particularly for the maximum surface-area-specific assimilation rate, \(\{\dot p_{Am}\}\), and the maximum ingestion rate, \([\dot F_m]\). However, these parameters cannot be compared independently of the relationship between structural length and fresh body mass. The two formulations also differ in the initial energy allocated to each cocoon, estimated at 131 J by Gergs et al. (2022) and 57.8 J in the present model. For a 0.5 g earthworm under ad libitum feeding, the resulting maximum assimilation fluxes are approximately 146 J\(\cdot\)d\(^{-1}\) in the present model and 106 J\(\cdot\)d\(^{-1}\) in Gergs et al. (2022). These differences highlight the importance of evaluating DEB parameterizations not only from their fit to life-history data, but also from their consistency with independent physiological measurements and the amount of energy available in the experimental system.
Parameter compensation and identifiability issues are common in DEB model calibration, particularly for ingestion- and assimilation-related parameters that integrate multiple physiological processes (Lika & Kooijman, 2011). In the present model, this issue is particularly relevant for the parameters governing energy acquisition. The digestion efficiency (\(\kappa_X\)) was fixed based on nitrogen assimilation efficiencies reported by Whalen & Parmelee (1999), but this value remains uncertain and may vary with the type and quality of ingested organic matter. Moreover, \(\kappa_X\) is mathematically closely linked to the maximum searching rate (\([\dot{F}_m]\)), since both parameters determine the amount of energy ultimately assimilated from ingested material. As a result, these parameters may partly compensate each other during calibration. Consistent with this interpretation, a strong posterior correlation was observed between \([\dot{F}_m]\) and \(K\), indicating that the maximum searching rate and the curvature of the functional response also partly compensate each other.
Together, these results suggest that \([\dot{F}_m]\), \(\kappa_X\), and \(K\) should be interpreted cautiously as effective parameters describing overall energy acquisition rather than as independent direct measurements of ingestion, digestion, or assimilation processes. This highlights the need for additional experimental data on ingestion, egestion, gut transit time, organic matter selection, and digestion efficiency to better constrain the mechanistic link between environmental organic matter and assimilated energy. The sensitivity analysis further showed that uncertainty in energy acquisition propagates beyond individual-level endpoints to environmental resource dynamics. Under the selected scenario, the amount of organic matter remaining in the cosm was influenced by several parameters governing allocation, assimilation, growth, and food acquisition, notably the fraction of energy allocated to soma during the juvenile phase (\(\kappa_J\)), the surface-specific maximum assimilation rate (\(\{\dot{p}_{Am}\}\)), the cost of structure (\(E_G\)), the structure weight-specific maximum searching rate (\([\dot{F}_m]\)), and the ratio between \(\{\dot{p}_{Am}\}\) and \([\dot p_M]\). This broad sensitivity profile indicates that organic matter depletion integrates both resource acquisition and the resulting energetic demand of the organism, rather than reflecting ingestion alone.
The present results also suggest that reserve contribution to fresh body mass is relatively very limited in A. caliginosa. The formulation assuming reserve mass independent of structural size consistently outperformed alternatives where reserve contribution scaled proportionally with structure. Similar formulations have been used in other DEB applications to better represent body mass dynamics under variable feeding conditions (Dortel et al., 2020). In addition, experiment Bart2019_XP3 showed little decrease in fresh body mass during periods where reserves were expected to decline, suggesting that reserve depletion contributes only weakly to total wet mass under the tested conditions.

title: 8  Discussion & Conclusion
text:
8.3 Energy allocation and the \(\kappa\) rule
The model comparison strongly supported formulations including a progressive transition in energy allocation after maturation. Models assuming a fixed allocation rule throughout the life cycle systematically produced poorer fits and resulted in unrealistic estimates for the energy content of cocoons. In contrast, introducing a gradual transition in allocation over a characteristic timescale \(\tau\) substantially improved model performance. The sensitivity analysis confirmed the central role of energy allocation in determining life-history trajectories. When temperature-related parameters were excluded, the juvenile allocation fraction (\(\kappa_J\)) was the main driver of body mass, maturity, and reproduction, at both juvenile and adult stages. Its influence across several endpoints shows that uncertainty in the allocation rule can propagate simultaneously to growth, maturation, and reproductive predictions.
These results provide an intermediate interpretation between the standard DEB \(\kappa\)-rule and alternative energy-budget formulations proposed for earthworms. Johnston et al. (2014) argued that reproduction should take priority over growth in adults and therefore rejected the standard DEB assumption of a constant allocation fraction. In contrast, Rakel et al. (2020) showed that the standard DEB model could adequately reproduce several experimental datasets when density effects were interpreted as competition for food and crowding rather than as changes in allocation strategy. More recently, Gergs et al. (2022) reproduced the growth plateau observed when adults were grouped by introducing different functional response values between juvenile and grouped-adult phases, effectively modifying energy assimilation after grouping.
Our results suggest that neither a strictly constant nor an instantaneous allocation shift fully captures the observed dynamics. The progressive transition introduced here allowed the model to better reproduce the smoother growth trajectories observed in the new density experiments, where juveniles were maintained in groups from the beginning of the experiment. In contrast, experiments from Bart (2019) displayed a sharper transition between juvenile growth and adult plateau, likely because adults were grouped only after maturity had been detected. Importantly, in these experiments, individuals experience a transient period during which they are physiologically mature but still isolated, because pairing occurs only after the experimenter identifies adulthood. During this interval, worms are effectively in an “isolated adult” state, with reproductive opportunities still absent. In the present model, this situation is represented by maintaining the juvenile allocation fraction (\(\kappa_J\)) until grouping occurs, after which a progressive transition toward the adult allocation fraction (\(\kappa_A\)) is initiated.
More generally, these results are consistent with the view that energy allocation may shift during ontogeny as organisms transition from growth-dominated juvenile stages to reproductive adult stages. Such stage-dependent allocation patterns have been documented in other organisms, for instance in Daphnia magna, where age affects the balance between somatic growth and reproductive investment (Glazier & Calow, 1992). These shifts also fit within the broader framework of life-history trade-offs, in which organisms allocate limited resources among competing functions such as growth, maintenance, and reproduction (Zera & Harshman, 2001). In A. caliginosa, the progressive transition in \(\kappa\) may therefore reflect both physiological changes associated with maturation and delays associated with the establishment of reproductive interactions.
The sensitivity analysis further showed that the representation of energy allocation is a major determinant of model behaviour. When temperature-related parameters were excluded, (\(\kappa_J\)) was the main driver of body mass, maturity, and reproduction at both juvenile and adult stages. Its influence across several endpoints indicates that uncertainty in juvenile allocation propagates throughout the life cycle, including after the transition toward the adult allocation strategy. This result supports the importance of accurately constraining allocation parameters, while also showing that several life-history predictions depend on a common underlying allocation mechanism.
Simulations of isolated adults highlighted limitations in the current representation of post-maturation energy allocation. Maintaining the juvenile allocation fraction throughout adulthood (\(\kappa_J\)) reproduced the observed growth trajectories more accurately than introducing a transition toward the adult allocation fraction (\(\kappa_A\)), which systematically underestimated growth after maturation. This suggests that isolated adults retain growth dynamics closer to those of juveniles than to those of grouped reproducing adults.
However, both formulations still predicted a non-zero reproductive flux after maturation despite the absence of observed cocoon production. This discrepancy raises the question of the energetic fate of reproduction-related fluxes in isolated individuals. One possible interpretation is that isolated adults still undergo physiological changes associated with maturation, including maturity maintenance costs, but that the energy normally allocated to reproduction is partly redirected toward somatic growth or reserve dynamics in the absence of mating opportunities. Alternatively, this energy may simply be dissipated rather than reallocated to another physiological function. More generally, these results suggest that isolated adults represent a distinct physiological state that is not fully captured by the current DEB formulations.
However, the ecological relevance of isolated adults remains limited. Under natural conditions, complete reproductive isolation is likely rare except at very low population densities. Consequently, the isolated-adult experiments should primarily be viewed as a useful conceptual framework for exploring energy allocation dynamics rather than as a realistic representation of field conditions.

title: 8  Discussion & Conclusion
text:
8.4 Model limitations and perspectives
Despite generally good agreement between simulations and observations, some systematic discrepancies remained. Growth plateaus were under or overestimated in some grouped adult experiments, and the transition between juvenile and adult growth remained more abrupt in several density treatments than in observations.
The model also did not reproduce the reduction in reproductive output observed for grouped individuals under low-food conditions (Bart2019_XP4_2) when density increased from three to six individuals per cosm under non-ad libitum feeding conditions. However, this effect was observed in only a single experimental condition, preventing robust incorporation of an explicit density-dependent reproductive process into the model. Reproductive output was also overestimated for individuals at density 2 with increased food supply (Gollot2026_D2b), where observed reproduction remained lower than predicted despite high food availability. This suggests that increasing food availability does not necessarily translate into proportional increases in reproduction and that additional processes, such as reproductive timing, individual variability, or microenvironmental effects, may influence cocoon production. As discussed above, the underestimation of juvenile growth at high population densities suggests that the assumption of homogeneous resource sharing may be too simplistic.
Overall, these discrepancies likely reflect processes that are not explicitly represented in the current formulation. First, effects of density may not be exclusively mediated by resource limitation. Behavioural interactions, spatial interference, or asymmetric competition may influence ingestion and reproduction. Second, variability among individuals in maturation timing may smooth the population-level transition between juvenile and adult stages, whereas the current model assumes homogeneous transition dynamics. Third, the quantification of ingestion and assimilation processes in endogeic earthworms remains highly uncertain because individuals feed directly within the soil matrix. Consequently, the ingestion-related parameters likely integrate multiple processes, including soil exploration, ingestion, digestion, gut transit, and assimilation efficiency.
The sensitivity analysis also highlighted the strong influence of temperature correction on model predictions. When thermal parameters were included, \(T_{\mathrm{ref}}\) and \(T_H\) dominated the sensitivity of most endpoints, and total-order indices were frequently much larger than first-order indices. This indicates substantial interactions between temperature correction, energy allocation, and other physiological processes. Accurate characterization of thermal dependence is therefore essential before applying the model across variable temperature regimes.
Future work should therefore focus on improving the mechanistic representation of energy acquisition and the thermal dependence of physiological rates in earthworms. In particular, experiments manipulating both the quantity and energetic quality of organic matter sources would help disentangle the respective roles of food quantity, food quality, and resource accessibility. Characterizing the energetic value of different organic amendments and soil organic matter fractions could further improve the mechanistic representation of assimilation processes and the estimation of functional response parameters. Simultaneous monitoring of organic matter depletion, ingestion, defecation, and cocoon production would also provide valuable constraints for assimilation-related parameters and the functional response.

title: 8  Discussion & Conclusion
text:
8.5 Conclusion
This study developed a Dynamic Energy Budget model for Aporrectodea caliginosa integrating the effects of food availability, organic matter quality, and population density on growth, maturation, and reproduction. By combining literature datasets with new density experiments performed from the juvenile stage onward, the model was calibrated across a broader range of life stages and environmental conditions than previous earthworm DEB studies.
The results indicate that reduced juvenile growth at higher densities can largely be explained by lower per-capita resource availability and food acquisition, without requiring an explicit density-dependent effect on energy assimilation. In contrast, the best-performing formulations also showed that post-maturation energy allocation cannot be adequately described by a strictly constant allocation rule throughout the life cycle. Introducing a progressive transition in energy allocation after maturation substantially improved the description of adult growth and reproduction trajectories, suggesting that reproductive opportunities shape energetic allocation in adult earthworms.
A major contribution of this work is the mechanistic linkage established between the functional response and environmental organic matter availability. The model explicitly distinguishes the energetic contribution of horse dung and soil organic matter, highlighting the limited assimilable energetic value of native soil organic matter relative to fresh organic amendments. The study also emphasizes the methodological difficulties associated with quantifying ingestion and assimilation processes in endogeic earthworms, which remain important limitations for mechanistic modelling approaches.
Overall, the proposed framework improves the ecological realism of DEB modelling for soil invertebrates by strengthening the links between environmental variability and individual energetics. This work provides a robust basis for future developments integrating multiple stressors, including pesticides and climate-related constraints, within DEB-TKTD modelling approaches for earthworms.

The juvenile growth experiments were conducted with juvenile individuals housed individually in cosms containing 200 g of Closeaux soil, maintained at 18°C, and fed 3 g of horse dung per individual every 14 days. Individuals were exposed to a range of concentrations of either imidacloprid or epoxiconazole. In the DEB-TKTD model, the initial maturity of these individuals must be specified, although it was not and can not be directly measured. 9.2.2 Re-estimations of \(\{\dot{p}_{Am}\}\), \(E_{coc}\) and \(\kappa_A\)
DEB parameter values were initially fixed at the modes of their posterior distributions obtained during the original model calibration (Chapter 6). Because discrepancies were observed between model predictions and the control data from the single-substance experiments, three DEB parameters associated with the biological processes requiring adjustment were recalibrated: the maximum surface-area-specific assimilation rate, \(\{\dot p_{Am}\}\), the cocoon energy content, \(E_{coc}\), and the adult allocation fraction, \(\kappa_A\). These parameters were selected based on their mechanistic relationships with the affected responses, while limiting the number of re-estimated parameters to preserve identifiability. Prior distributions were defined within \(\pm 30%\) of the values obtained during the initial DEB calibration. The posterior mode estimates of \(\{\dot p_{Am}\}\), \(E_{coc}\), and \(\kappa_A\) were subsequently fixed during the calibration of the DEB-TKTD models.

Figure 9.8: Observed growth and reproduction responses of control Aporrectodea caliginosa and corresponding predictions from the baseline DEB model before and after parameter recalibration. Points represent experimental treatment means. The original trajectories were generated using the posterior mode parameter values from the initial DEB calibration, whereas the recalibrated trajectories used the newly estimated values of the allocation energy fraction to soma in adults (\(\kappa_A\)).





Predictions obtained with the original DEB parameterization showed a slight underestimation of both juvenile and adult growth, together with an overestimation of cocoon production (Figure 9.8). To improve the description of the control trajectories before estimating toxicodynamic effects, three DEB parameters were therefore re-estimated: the maximum surface-area-specific assimilation rate, \(\{\dot{p}_{Am}\}\), the cocoon energy content, \(E_{coc}\), and the adult allocation fraction, \(\kappa_A\).
The posterior mode of \(\{\dot{p}_{Am}\}\) increased from 259.9 [234.8 ; 285.7] to 341.8 [267.5; 377.2] J\(\cdot\)cm\(^{-2}\cdot\)d\(^{-1}\), while \(E_{coc}\) increased from 57.8 [51.2 ; 70.0] to 75.0 [51.8; 114.2] J. The posterior mode of \(\kappa_A\) also increased slightly, from 0.71 [0.63 ; 0.76] to 0.73 [0.69; 0.77]. The substantial overlap between the original and recalibrated credible intervals indicates that the updated estimates remained broadly consistent with the initial DEB parameterization. The posterior correlation between the parameters was weak, indicating that the parameters were estimated independently (Figure 9.6).
Using the recalibrated parameter values improved the agreement between predicted and observed juvenile and adult growth trajectories. Reproduction was also more closely reproduced than with the original parameterization, although cocoon production remained slightly overestimated. However, the recalibration also resulted in wider 95% credible intervals, indicating greater uncertainty in the predicted responses. The posterior mode estimates of \(\{\dot{p}_{Am}\}\), \(E_{coc}\), and \(\kappa_A\) were nevertheless retained and fixed for all subsequent DEB-TKTD analyses.

title: 9  Data and adjustments
text:
9.3 Construction of the DEB-TKTD models

9.3.1 Toxicokinetic models
Internal concentrations of epoxiconazole and imidacloprid are simulated using previously developed toxicokinetic models (more details here). For both compounds, two-compartment TK formulations were retained and parameterized using the median of posterior parameter distributions estimated from dedicated bioaccumulation experiments. External exposure concentrations corresponded to analytically measured soil concentrations rather than nominal concentrations. The TK models were originally calibrated under nominal exposure conditions of 100 ng.g\(^{-1}\) dry soil for imidacloprid and 1000 ng.g\(^{-1}\) dry soil for epoxiconazole.
Because previous toxicokinetic analyses found no evidence for mixture-related TK interactions between epoxiconazole and imidacloprid, single-substance TK models are used unchanged to simulate internal concentrations under co-exposure scenarios. Consequently, each compound is assumed to follow independent uptake and elimination dynamics in mixture conditions.
Previous toxicokinetic analyses identified concentration-dependent deviations for imidacloprid, with evidence of saturation occurring at internal concentrations around 1676 ng.g\(^{-1}\). Under the original first-order formulation, this saturation implied a restricted application domain, corresponding to external concentrations below approximately 80 ng.g\(^{-1}\) dry soil assuming a bioaccumulation factor of 21. However, because several exposure concentrations used in the toxicity experimental data exceeded the external concentration range over which the initial TK model could be applied, this saturation process is explicitly incorporated into the imidacloprid toxicokinetic module. The TK model for imidacloprid is therefore modified to account for a plateau in internal concentrations at high exposure levels, preventing unrealistic linear increases in internal exposure beyond the observed saturation range. This extended formulation is used for all imidacloprid-related simulations and parameter inferences in the DEB-TKTD model.


9.3.2 Toxicodynamic model and physiological modes of action
Toxicodynamic processes is modeled following a standard DEB-TKTD formulation in which internal concentrations generate a damage variable that translates into physiological stress affecting DEB energetic fluxes (Baas et al., 2018; Jager et al., 2006; Jager et al., 2023) (Equation 9.1). Because no toxicokinetic interactions are assumed, separate damage dynamics are modeled for epoxiconazole and imidacloprid, each compound being characterized by its own toxicodynamic parameters.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm d D}{\mathrm d t} &= k_r (C_{\mathrm{int}} - D) \\ \\
s &= b(D−c_0)
\end{aligned}
\tag{9.1}\]
with :

\(C_{\mathrm{int}}\) : the internal concentration,
\(D\) : the internal damage scaled in the same unit as \(C_{\mathrm{int}}\),
\(k_r\) : Recuperation or repair constant of damage.$,
\(s\) : the stress factor,
\(b\) : damage sensitivity (\(b = 1/c_T\) with \(c_T\) the tolerance concentration),
\(c_0\) : the no-effect concentration.

To reduce parameter identifiability issues, the damage recovery constant (\(k_r\)) was fixed to 1, so that damage instantaneously followed the internal concentration (\(D=C_{\mathrm{int}}\)).
For each pesticide, multiple physiological modes of action (pMoA) are evaluated individually by allowing toxic stress to alter different DEB processes, including assimilation, maintenance, growth, maturation, and reproduction (Table 9.1).



Table 9.1: Accounting for the different possible physiological modes of action in a DEB model. The stress factor \(s\) is defined as a linear threshold damage function based on a no-effect concentration (\(c_0\)), whose inverse slope is commonly referred to as the tolerance concentration (\(c_T\)) (Kooijman et al., 2009). Adapted from Table 2 in Jager et al. (2023).










Physiological mode of action (pMoA)
Affected parameters
Effect on parameters




Ingestion and/or assimilation
\(\{\dot{p}_{Am}\}\): Surface-area-specific assimilation flux (J d\(^{-1}\) cm\(^{-2}\))
\(\{\dot{p}_{Am}\} \rightarrow (1-s)\{\dot{p}_{Am}\}\)



or




\(f\): Functional response (-)
\(f \rightarrow f_0 \max(0,1-s)\)


Maintenance costs
\([\dot{p}_M]\): Volume-specific somatic maintenance flux (J d\(^{-1}\) cm\(^{-3}\))
\([\dot{p}_M] \rightarrow (1+s)[\dot{p}_M]\)



\(\dot{k}_J\): Maturity maintenance rate coefficient (d\(^{-1}\))
\(\dot{k}_J \rightarrow (1+s)\dot{k}_J\)


Growth and maturity costs
\(E_G\): Volume-specific cost of structure (J g\(^{-1}\))
\(E_G \rightarrow (1+s)E_G\)



\(\kappa_H\): Maturation efficiency (= 1 in the standard DEB model)
\(\kappa_H \rightarrow \kappa_H/(1+s)\)


Reproduction costs
\(\kappa_R\): Reproduction efficiency
\(\kappa_R \rightarrow \kappa_R/(1+s)\)


Embryo damage
\(\kappa_R\): Reproduction efficiency
\(\kappa_R \rightarrow \exp(-s)\kappa_R\)






Candidate pMoAs are first evaluated independently for each compound and subsequently combined for the most supported hypotheses. Competing models are compared using the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), allowing comparison among alternative physiological hypotheses while penalizing model complexity.
Models are designated in the code with combinaison of letters corresponding to the pMoA(s) considered in a given model :

A : Ingestion and/or Assimilation costs,
M : Maintenance costs,
G : Growth and maturity costs,
R : Reproduction costs.

Both the DEB recalibration and the DEB-TKTD calibration on the single substances data Gollot et al. (2026) were performed using Bayesian inference implemented in MCSim (Bois, 2009). Three independent Markov chain Monte Carlo chains of 30,000 iterations were run, and the final 10,000 iterations of each chain were retained to characterize the posterior distributions. Growth endpoints were modeled assuming normally distributed residuals, whereas cocoon production was modeled using a Poisson likelihood. Convergence was assessed by inspecting chain mixing and the agreement of posterior distributions among chains. Point estimates were defined as the modes of the posterior distributions with their 95% credibility intervals.

Figure 10.23: Predicted Weight and Reproduction for exposure condition.





Overall, the selected DEB-TKTD model reproduced the concentration-dependent responses observed for juvenile growth, adult growth, and reproduction (Figure 10.23, Figure 10.19 & fig-pred_G_EPX_ARsummary). The model captured the general magnitude and shape of the decline in life-history performance with increasing epoxiconazole exposure. However, some systematic deviations remained. Growth was underestimated at the lowest tested concentrations, between 0.928 and 9.28 mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\). Reproductive effects were also underestimated at the highest concentrations, between 43.1 and 200 mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\), with predicted cocoon production exceeding the observed values. Despite these discrepancies, the combined assimilation and reproduction pMoA provided an overall satisfactory description of epoxiconazole effects across the three endpoints.

Predicted internal epoxiconazole concentrations increased approximately proportionally with external exposure concentration (Figure 10.24, Table 10.2). Maximum internal concentrations were generally reached within the first 4-6 days of exposure, considerably earlier than for imidacloprid, and were slightly higher in adults than in juveniles. The estimated no-effect concentration of 47,101 ng\(\cdot\)g\(^{-1}\) was exceeded only at the two highest exposure concentrations, 92.8 and 200 mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\). At 20.0 mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\) and 43.1 mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\), the predicted maximum internal concentration was below the median estimate of the no-effect threshold. However, given the wide credible interval around \(c_0\), this exposure condition may still exceed the threshold for part of the posterior distribution.

format_summary <- function(df) {
  df %>%
    rename_with(~ str_remove(., "\\.1\\.$")) %>%
    rownames_to_column("stat") %>%
    pivot_longer(
      cols = -c(stat, Model),
      names_to = "param",
      values_to = "value"
    ) %>%
    pivot_wider(
      names_from = stat,
      values_from = value
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      value = str_c(
        round(Result_mode, 4),
        " [", round(`2.5%`, 4),
        " ; ", round(`97.5%`, 4), "]"
      )
    ) %>%
    dplyr::select(Model, param, value) %>%
    pivot_wider(
      names_from = param,
      values_from = value
    )
}

Table 11.1: Estimation results from all models.










For imidacloprid, the lowest BIC was obtained for the model combining effects on maintenance and growth (BIC = -65.1; Table 11.1). However, the assimilation-and-growth formulation received nearly equivalent support (BIC = -64.1; \(\Delta\mathrm{BIC}=1.0\)), whereas the growth-and-reproduction model was less supported (BIC = -62.8; \(\Delta\mathrm{BIC}=2.3\)). The remaining formulations showed substantially higher BIC values. These results therefore did not allow a clear statistical distinction between the maintenance-and-growth and assimilation-and-growth pMoAs. Because imidacloprid is known to affect earthworm activity, feeding behaviour, and bioturbation (Dittbrenner et al., 2010), a reduction in resource acquisition or processing was considered biologically more plausible than a primary increase in maintenance costs. The assimilation-and-growth formulation was therefore retained for subsequent analyses, while acknowledging the maintenance-and-growth model as an equally plausible statistical alternative.
The selected assimilation and growth model estimated a no-effect concentration (\(c_0\)) of 1,132 [882; 1,494] ng\(\cdot\)g\(^{-1}\) internal concentration and a stress slope parameter (\(b\)) of 0.02 [0.01; 8.54] g\(\cdot\)ng\(^{-1}\). The wide credible interval around \(b\) indicates that the increase in stress above the threshold remained poorly constrained.

Overall, the selected DEB-TKTD model captured the main concentration-response patterns observed for juvenile growth, adult growth, and reproduction (Figure 11.23, Figure 11.19 & Figure 11.21). It reproduced the general decline in life-history performance with increasing imidacloprid exposure, supporting a physiological mode of action involving both reduced assimilation and altered growth processes.

The model overestimated the effect on juvenile growth at intermediate imidacloprid concentrations (0.158 and 0.5 mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\)) resulting in predicted values below the observations. Reproduction was similarly underestimated over this intermediate concentration range. At the highest concentrations, between 1.6 and 5 mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\), the model moderately underestimated the effect on growth and cocoon production.

Predicted internal concentrations increased throughout the 28-day exposure at the four lowest imidacloprid concentrations, with maximum values reached at the end of the experiment (Figure 11.24, Table 11.2). title: 12  Discussion & Conclusions
text:
12.1 Single compound effect
The DEB-TKTD analysis confirmed the marked difference in toxicity between imidacloprid and epoxiconazole observed in Aporrectodea caliginosa, for which reproduction EC\(_{50}\) values were previously estimated at 0.55 and 126.8 mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\) for imidacloprid and epoxiconazole, respectively (Gollot et al., 2026). The internal no-effect concentrations was estimated at 1,132 [882 ; 1,494] ng\(\cdot\)g\(^{-1}\) for imidacloprid, compared with 47,101 [14,367; 96,352] ng\(\cdot\)g\(^{-1}\) for epoxiconazole, indicating that physiological stress was initiated at a substantially lower internal exposure for imidacloprid. This difference is consistent with the literature with reported reproduction EC\(_{50}\) values of 0.21-1.89 mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\) in Eisenia species, depending on soil properties and experimental conditions (Bandeira et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019).
At toxicokinetic equilibrium, the internal no-effect concentrations can be translated into approximate external soil concentrations using the bioaccumulation factors previously estimated for the two compounds. Based on a bioaccumulation factor of 21, the imidacloprid no-effect concentration corresponds to an external concentration of approximately 0.055 [0.042 ; 0.071] mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\). For epoxiconazole, using a bioaccumulation factor of 0.9, the corresponding external concentration is approximately 52.3 [15.9 ; 107.1] mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\). These external-equivalent thresholds are consistent with the concentration ranges over which effects were observed experimentally and further illustrate the much greater potency of imidacloprid. However, these conversions should be interpreted cautiously because they assume constant exposure and toxicokinetic equilibrium.
From an environmental perspective, the external-equivalent threshold estimated for imidacloprid, 0.055 [0.042; 0.071] mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\), is higher than the median concentrations reported in soils, which ranged from 0.0029 to 0.020 mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\), but remains below the highest measured values of 0.060 and 0.160 mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\) (Froger et al., 2023; Pelosi et al., 2021; Silva et al., 2019). This indicates that peak contamination levels may exceed the concentration associated with the onset of toxic stress. In contrast, the external-equivalent threshold estimated for epoxiconazole, 52.3 [15.9; 107.1] mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\), remains far above reported soil concentrations, with medians ranging from 0.0058 to 0.0346 mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\) and maxima from 0.0236 to 0.283 mg\(\cdot\)kg\(^{-1}\) (Froger et al., 2023; Pelosi et al., 2021; Silva et al., 2019). These comparisons suggest a much narrower environmental safety margin for imidacloprid than for epoxiconazole under current contamination scenarios.

title: 12  Discussion & Conclusions
text:
12.2 Physiological modes of action
For both pesticides, several physiological modes of action received similar statistical support, and model selection therefore relied on both BIC values and biological plausibility. For imidacloprid, the maintenance-and-growth formulation had the lowest BIC, but the assimilation-and-growth model was statistically equivalent and was retained because known effects of imidacloprid on earthworm activity, feeding, and bioturbation support a disturbance of resource acquisition (Table 11.1). For epoxiconazole, the growth-and-reproduction model had the lowest BIC, but the assimilation-and-reproduction formulation received virtually identical support and was retained as a biologically plausible representation of the documented effects of epoxiconazole on energy reserves and reproductive performance (Table 10.1). Assimilation therefore emerged as a plausible component of the response to both compounds, although the available data did not allow the respective contributions of assimilation, maintenance, growth, and reproduction to be identified unambiguously.
More generally, comparison of alternative pMoAs within a DEB-TKTD framework should be regarded primarily as a screening approach for identifying the energetic processes that are most consistent with the observed life-history responses. Statistical support alone is generally insufficient to establish the underlying physiological mechanism, particularly when several pMoAs generate similar growth and reproduction trajectories. Additional physiological measurements are therefore required to discriminate among competing hypotheses and strengthen their biological interpretation. For example, in a multigenerational study of uranium toxicity in Daphnia magna, both reduced assimilation and increased maintenance costs were initially considered as possible explanations for the observed effects, but independent measurements of carbon assimilation and alterations of the digestive epithelium provided additional support for impaired assimilation (Massarin et al., 2011). This illustrates how DEB-TKTD model comparison can guide the formulation of mechanistic hypotheses, which must subsequently be evaluated using complementary physiological evidence (Péry et al., 2002).
The biological interpretation of these functional pMoAs is nevertheless consistent with known effects of the two compounds.
Imidacloprid is a neuroactive pesticide that can alter activity, feeding behaviour and burrowing in earthworms, while also affecting detoxification pathways and cellular integrity (Dittbrenner et al., 2010; Kaur et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2019; Zang et al., 2000). Reduced feeding or food processing could therefore be represented in the DEB model as impaired assimilation. However, reduced assimilation and increased maintenance costs can produce qualitatively similar effects on growth and reproduction, because both decrease the amount of energy available for growth and reproductive investment (Jager, 2015). Energetic costs associated with detoxification, maintenance of homeostasis and cellular repair could therefore also contribute to the observed responses, even though the maintenance-based formulation was not retained. The additional effect on growth may represent more specific alterations of tissue production or an increase in the energetic cost of building new structure. Distinguishing among these processes would require complementary measurements of food consumption, assimilation efficiency, respiration or energy reserves.
Epoxiconazole exposure has been associated with oxidative stress, depletion of energetic reserves and reduced reproductive performance in earthworms (Bart et al., 2019, 2020; Givaudan, 2014; Pelosi et al., 2016). These effects are consistent with a disturbance of energy acquisition or availability, which could be represented in the DEB model as impaired assimilation. Epoxiconazole and other azole fungicides can also interfere with steroid biosynthesis and hormone signalling in vertebrate systems, resulting in reproductive and developmental effects (ECHA, 2025; Kjærstad et al., 2010; Taxvig et al., 2007; Zarn et al., 2003). Although these mechanisms cannot be directly extrapolated to earthworms, they support the biological plausibility of an additional perturbation of reproductive processes contributing to the observed response. However, the nearly equivalent support for the growth-and-reproduction formulation indicates that a direct effect on growth remains an equally plausible alternative.
Within the present DEB-TKTD framework, however, such mechanisms are represented through changes in energetic fluxes rather than modeled explicitly. The selected pMoAs should therefore be interpreted as functional descriptions of the processes required to reproduce the observed life-history responses, rather than as direct evidence for specific biochemical mechanisms.
Accurate representation of control responses was an important prerequisite for estimating pesticide effects within the DEB-TKTD framework. Differences between control observations and baseline model predictions may reflect both structural limitations of the model and the natural variability of biological responses, since the observed control means represent only one realization of the underlying distribution. A discrepancy in the point predictions is therefore not necessarily problematic when the observations remain compatible with the associated predictive uncertainty. Conversely, a systematic deviation across endpoints or time points may be incorrectly attributed to toxic stress and thereby bias estimates of the no-effect concentration, stress slope and physiological mode of action.
In the present study, the original DEB parameterization slightly underestimated juvenile and adult growth while overestimating cocoon production. Re-estimating the maximum surface-area-specific assimilation rate, \(\{\dot{p}_{Am}\}\), the cocoon energy content, \(E_{coc}\), and the adult allocation fraction, \(\kappa_A\), from the control data improved the representation of baseline growth and reproduction before fitting the toxicodynamic parameters. Limiting recalibration to parameters mechanistically related to the affected responses also reduced the risk of overfitting and preserved parameter identifiability. Although the recalibrated model slightly overestimated the central estimate of cocoon production, the observed value remained within the model credibility interval. Consequently, the support for a direct reproductive pMoA for epoxiconazole is unlikely to result solely from a clear mismatch in the baseline model, although some residual uncertainty in the representation of control reproduction remains.
More generally, these results emphasize that DEB-TKTD calibration should first verify that control responses are adequately represented, together with their variability and uncertainty, before compound-specific toxicodynamic processes are inferred.

title: 12  Discussion & Conclusions
section: 12.3 Model limitations and perspective of improvement
text:
12.3 Model limitations and perspective of improvement
The selected models generally captured the concentration-dependent responses in juvenile growth, adult growth, and reproduction, although some systematic deviations remained for both compounds. For epoxiconazole, the combined assimilation and reproduction model reproduced the overall response patterns but underestimated growth effects at the lowest tested concentrations and reproductive effects at the highest concentrations. These discrepancies remained relatively limited, but they indicate that the selected pMoA did not fully capture the shape of the response across the entire exposure gradient. For imidacloprid, the model underestimated juvenile growth and reproduction at intermediate concentrations, while cocoon production was slightly overestimated at the highest concentrations.
Several processes may contribute to these residual patterns. First, the threshold-linear stress function may be too restrictive to describe a nonlinear or relatively abrupt transition between low and pronounced effects. Alternative formulations, such as a Hill-type stress function, could provide greater flexibility in the shape of the toxicodynamic response. Second, imidacloprid toxicokinetics showed evidence of saturation at high exposure levels, restricting the application domain of the TK model. Internal concentrations, and consequently toxic effects, may therefore be less accurately predicted for the highest treatments. Finally, adult mortality observed at the highest imidacloprid concentration could not be reproduced because survival was not explicitly represented in the present model. Predictions at this concentration therefore describe only sublethal growth and reproduction processes and do not account for the loss of individuals during exposure.
Although the estimated no-effect concentrations provide a mechanistically relevant measure of sensitivity, their credible intervals remained relatively broad, particularly for epoxiconazole. This uncertainty likely results partly from the distribution of tested concentrations. Relatively few treatments were located close to the inferred onset of effects, whereas many observations corresponded either to concentrations producing little response or to concentrations already associated with marked toxicity. Additional experimental treatments concentrated around the estimated no-effect concentrations would improve identification of the threshold and help distinguish more clearly between competing pMoAs.
The available experimental data also covered separate and very restricted portions of the life cycle rather than following individuals continuously from hatching to adulthood and reproduction. Endpoints were measured over a short period, with juvenile growth assessed at only three time points, adult growth at two time points, and cocoon production at a single time point over 28 days. This limited temporal resolution makes it difficult to distinguish among physiological modes of action, as several pMoAs may produce similar responses over short exposure periods but differ in their longer-term effects on ultimate size, maturation timing, or reproductive rate (Jager, 2015). Combining these endpoints within a single DEB-TKTD framework provides a more integrated analysis than endpoint-specific dose-response models, but it does not fully constrain the temporal propagation of toxic effects across the life cycle. Experiments following individuals from emergence to maturity and reproduction under continuous exposure would provide stronger information on delayed maturation, carry-over effects, changes in energy allocation between life stages, and the discrimination among competing pMoAs.
Finally, effects on embryonic development could not be incorporated into the present model because the available data were insufficient to estimate an embryo-specific damage process. Although cocoon production was quantified, the model did not explicitly represent potential effects on cocoon quality, embryonic development time, hatching success, or hatchling condition. This limitation may be important because reproductive toxicity can arise not only through reduced maternal investment but also through direct exposure of cocoons and embryos. Future DEB-TKTD developments should therefore integrate embryonic development and hatching data, ideally within experiments covering the complete life cycle. Such data would allow discrimination between effects on adult energy allocation, cocoon production, and embryo viability, thereby improving both the mechanistic interpretation and predictive capacity of the model.

title: 12  Discussion & Conclusions
section: 12.4 Towards a DEB-TKTD for the mixture
text:
12.4 Towards a DEB-TKTD for the mixture
A first step toward a DEB-TKTD model for the mixture would be to predict combined effects directly from the independently calibrated single-compound models, without introducing an additional interaction parameter. This approach would provide a mechanistic reference prediction against which the observed mixture responses could be compared and would allow assessment of whether accounting explicitly for the toxicokinetics and physiological effects of each compound improves mixture predictions relative to conventional external concentration-based approaches.
Because no toxicokinetic interaction was detected between imidacloprid and epoxiconazole, their internal concentration dynamics can initially be simulated using the single-compound TK models. The resulting compound-specific internal concentrations would then generate separate damage and stress variables, which could be combined at the level of the affected DEB processes. Although both compounds were associated with reduced assimilation in the selected DEB-TKTD formulations, this common pMoA does not necessarily imply that they act through the same molecular or cellular target. A DEB pMoA represents an aggregated effect on an energetic flux and may encompass several distinct biochemical, behavioral, or physiological mechanisms. Imidacloprid and epoxiconazole could therefore still be considered independent at the underlying mechanism level, given their different primary modes of action.
Under an Independent Action assumption, the compound-specific stress modifiers can be combined multiplicatively. Thus, a DEB process modified by a factor \((1 \pm s)\) for a single compound would be modified by \((1 \pm s_{\mathrm{IMD}})(1 \pm s_{\mathrm{EPX}})\) under joint exposure (Jager et al., 2010; Matyja, 2023). The sign depends on whether stress increases or decreases the affected process.
This formulation preserves the separate TK and TD dynamics of each pesticide while generating a prediction of their combined effect in the absence of an explicit interaction. Comparing these predictions with the observed mixture data would help determine whether the apparent mixture response can be explained by independent physiological effects acting simultaneously or whether an additional interaction term is required.
The reliability of this approach nevertheless depends on the predictive performance of the single-compound models. The epoxiconazole model reproduced juvenile growth, adult growth, and reproduction without a strong systematic residual pattern, apart from a slight underestimation of growth effects at the highest concentrations. Its contribution to mixture predictions is therefore expected to be reasonably well characterized. In contrast, the imidacloprid model overestimated effects at intermediate concentrations and underestimated them at the highest concentrations. These systematic deviations may propagate into mixture predictions, leading to excessive predicted effects when the imidacloprid contribution is intermediate and insufficient predicted effects in mixtures dominated by high imidacloprid exposure. Consequently, discrepancies between observed and predicted mixture responses could reflect either a genuine interaction between compounds or limitations inherited from the single-compound model.
This issue is particularly important because imidacloprid is expected to drive much of the mixture toxicity owing to its substantially greater potency. Improving the description of its concentration–response pattern, especially at intermediate and high exposure levels, would therefore strengthen the interpretation of mixture predictions. Additional data around the transition between moderate and strong effects, together with a more explicit representation of high-concentration processes such as starvation (Jager et al., 2023) and mortality, could reduce this uncertainty.
Despite these limitations, generating mixture predictions from independently calibrated DEB-TKTD models would remain informative. It would test whether the integration of compound-specific internal exposure and time-dependent physiological stress provides a better description of mixture effects than approaches based solely on external concentrations. If the observed mixture responses were adequately reproduced, this would suggest that explicit interaction mechanisms are not required. Conversely, systematic deviations from the independent prediction could motivate the development of interaction terms acting on toxicokinetics, damage dynamics, stress intensity, or DEB energetic fluxes. In the longer term, this mixture DEB-TKTD framework could also be coupled with a mixture GUTS model to integrate lethal effects alongside sublethal effects on growth and reproduction. Such a coupling would provide a more comprehensive representation of pesticide mixture toxicity across individual-level endpoints, building on the mixture survival modeling approach developed by Bart et al. (2021).
